blocks.text: 1. Sigmoid

blocks.alt: Any real number passes through sigmoid into a value between 0 and 1

blocks.text: Step Function's fatal, zero-gradient flaw, covered in depth in the previous topic, motivated the search for something better. Sigmoid was the field's first genuine solution: a smooth curve with a usable, non-zero gradient across nearly its entire range.

Sigmoid was already previewed as the Output Layer's own binary classification activation, back in the Neural Network Fundamentals module. This topic covers it in full mathematical depth for the first time, explaining exactly why it works, and exactly where it genuinely falls short.
2. Sigmoid's Mathematics

blocks.alt: Input passes through 1 over 1 plus e to minus x

blocks.text: Sigmoid takes any real number as input, positive or negative, arbitrarily large or small, and squashes it into a smooth, S-shaped curve, the classic shape most people picture when they first hear the word sigmoid.

Its output is always strictly between 0 and 1, though it never actually reaches either endpoint exactly, no matter how extreme the input value becomes, always approaching but never quite touching those two boundary values.
3. A Smooth, Usable Gradient

blocks.alt: Sigmoid has a smooth, usable gradient

blocks.text: This directly solves the step function's fatal flaw, covered in the previous topic. Sigmoid's derivative is smooth and non-zero across nearly its entire range, giving backpropagation a genuinely usable signal to work with almost everywhere along the curve.

Its steepest gradient sits right around an input of zero, gradually flattening out toward both extremes as the input grows increasingly large or increasingly negative, a genuine improvement over the step function, though this flattening behavior itself becomes a real weakness covered later in this topic.

blocks.text: 4. The Probability Interpretation

This connects directly back to binary classification output, already covered in the Output Layer topic. Sigmoid's 0-to-1 output range maps naturally onto a probability, a genuinely intuitive interpretation that made it a natural first choice for this exact task.

An output of 0.85, for instance, means the model is genuinely 85 percent confident the input belongs to the positive class, a direct, immediately usable interpretation that considerably simplifies how a binary classification network's output actually gets read and acted on.
5. The Vanishing Gradient Problem

blocks.alt: A very large or small input produces a tiny gradient

blocks.text: A genuine, serious weakness, discovered through real, practical experience, is that for very large positive or very large negative inputs, sigmoid's curve flattens out almost completely, exactly the flattening behavior already previewed in an earlier section.

The gradient in these flattened regions becomes extremely small, though technically not exactly zero. This is called the vanishing gradient problem, covered in far more depth in the Backpropagation and Optimization module later in this course, a genuine, serious practical issue that emerges specifically in deep networks.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: The vanishing gradient problem is one of the single most important concepts in this entire course to understand clearly. It directly explains why sigmoid, despite solving the step function's original flaw, still fell out of favor for hidden layers.

blocks.text: 6. Impact on Deep Networks

blocks.alt: A tiny gradient multiplied across many layers vanishes to zero

blocks.text: In a deep network with many stacked sigmoid layers, these small gradients multiply together across every single layer during backpropagation, since the chain rule, covered in its own topic in the Backpropagation module ahead, combines gradients multiplicatively across layers.

The combined gradient actually reaching the network's early layers can become genuinely, vanishingly tiny after passing through many sigmoid layers in sequence. Early layers essentially stop learning at all under these conditions, a real, practical training failure that becomes considerably worse the deeper a sigmoid-based network actually is.
7. A Second Weakness: Not Zero-Centered

A second, less severe but genuinely real weakness is that sigmoid's output is never negative, always strictly between 0 and 1, a property called not being zero-centered, since its outputs do not naturally spread symmetrically around zero.

This can slow down training in specific, genuine ways, covered in further mathematical depth in the Backpropagation and Optimization module later in this course, a secondary but real concern beyond the more serious vanishing gradient problem already covered earlier in this topic.
8. Where Sigmoid Still Earns Its Place

blocks.alt: A binary classification output is where sigmoid is still used

blocks.text: Sigmoid still genuinely earns its place today as the output layer activation for binary classification, exactly as already covered in the Output Layer topic, since its 0-to-1 probability interpretation is precisely what that specific task genuinely needs.

For hidden layers in most modern networks, sigmoid has been largely replaced by ReLU and its variants, covered later in this module, specifically because of the vanishing gradient problem covered throughout this topic, a problem those alternative functions were specifically designed to avoid.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Sigmoid Is Genuinely Right
For the output layer of a binary classifier, sigmoid remains the standard, default choice today, directly connecting to the exact use case already covered fully in the Output Layer topic.

For a hidden layer in a genuinely deep network, sigmoid is generally best avoided, in favor of the alternatives covered later throughout this module, given the real, practical vanishing gradient problem already covered in depth throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Sigmoid was the field's first genuine solution to the step function's zero-gradient flaw.
It squashes any real number into a smooth S-shaped curve, output always strictly between 0 and 1.
Its smooth, mostly non-zero gradient gives backpropagation a genuinely usable signal, unlike the step function.
Its 0-to-1 output maps naturally onto a probability, e.g. 0.85 meaning 85 percent confidence.
For extreme inputs, sigmoid's gradient becomes extremely small, called the vanishing gradient problem.
In deep networks, these small gradients multiply across layers, causing early layers to essentially stop learning.
Sigmoid's output is never negative, a property called not zero-centered, which can slow training too.
Sigmoid remains standard for binary classification output layers, but is largely avoided for hidden layers today.
Next up: Tanh, a related function that fixes the not-zero-centered weakness while still facing vanishing gradients.
